newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's slain rebel chief lies in humble tomb.
newsitem.headline: Peru's slain rebel chief lies in humble tomb.

text.p: There is a rumour going round the "New Hope" slum graveyard that the tormented ghost of Peru's slain rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini prowls the sprawling cemetery at night.

If Cerpa did rise from the dead, he would have to slip plainclothes intelligence agents tapping their guns from a not-so-discrete distance because they keep vigil over the pauper's grave night and day.
He would also need to defy a huge concrete slab placed over his coffin to stop political enemies, or admirers, from snatching his corpse.
"They say he comes out at night. Do you believe it?" asks Isabel Porras, 29, kneeling beside her mother's grave on a dusty hummock opposite Cerpa's resting place.
"I've got four relatives in here. I want them to be peaceful. Why didn't they bury him somewhere else?"

Despite such unquiet, it is a fitting burial ground the government has chosen for Cerpa, a self-proclaimed defender of the poor. The former Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader, gunned down when troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's home on April 22 to rescue 72 hostages held for four months, would surely have approved.
His tomb, two-thirds of the way up a sand dune on a far edge of the cemetery, is indistinguishable from tens of thousands of other poor graves straggling the drab hillsides.

A black wooden cross reads simply: "May You Rest In Peace. Nestor Cerpa Cartolini. 22.4.97." A few flowers wilt in the sun, while a message with a white ribbon says: "God be with you on your road to glory. On earth, your brothers and sisters remember you and weep for you forever."

Among the scores of poor Peruvians mourning relatives or scraping a living in the New Hope graveyard, not many wept for Cerpa. But there was plenty of sympathy for the doomed Marxist revolutionary if not for his violent methods.

"He was a real fighter for the poor. There are few people prepared to stick their neck out for the poor like him," said 31-year-old Mercedes Gutierrez, who has sold drinks for eight years in the graveyard and, like others, was surprisingly eager to talk about Cerpa.
"The government will present him as a villain, but that is not the case. He just chose the wrong way, that's all."

The chaotic, immense municipal cemetery, which stretches limitlessly into the desert as more and more bodies are buried, is located beside the Villa Maria Del Triunfo shantytown in the heart of Lima's poverty belt.

The hillside shacks, stench of rubbish, mangy animals, and human scavengers picking over scraps in the road, dramatically illustrate the very poverty and marginalization Cerpa and the MRTA said motivated their armed struggle.

Inside the cemetery makeshift wooden crosses and piles of stones over most graves show poignantly how even in death many Peruvians have to skimp. Just the right to bury a loved one here costs $56, while a hole in the earth costs a further $30 - a total not far short of the minimum monthly wage.
A few dashes of colour, where some relatives have left flowers or built a tiny chapel, break the graveyard's monotony.

Cerpa, who died at 43, was born into a working-class family, left school at 17, and later joined a group of union leaders at the Cromotex textile plant. During one protest, police killed six workers including Cerpa's mentor, union leader Hemigidio Huertas, arresting and beating many others.

Upon release from jail he went underground and helped organise the Cuban-inspired MRTA in the early 1980s. He rose to its leadership in the mid-1990s after his superiors were captured, and masterminded the brilliantly executed takeover of the Japanese ambassador's home on Dec. 17, 1996.

Cerpa named himself "Comandante Huertas" and frequently invoked the Cromotex incident as he and 13 other jungle-trained rebels, including teenagers and two girls, initially took 500 people hostages. The captors released all women and elderly men, and held the remaining 72 hostages for 126 days.

Although prepared to die and kill for his cause, and with a string of bombings and kidnappings behind him, family members and former comrades remembered a shy, cautious man who favoured books over bullets and dialogue over death. Former hostages described him as courteous and cultured, while his passion for football and childish letters to his 10-year-old son in France showed his human side.

On April 22, Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's patience ran out, and in an ingenious military operation, troops exploded through tunnels into the home to kill the rebels and free all but one of the captives.
"He died for his cause. What on earth did they think they were doing in there?" mused gravedigger Julio Marca, 45, opposite Cerpa's grave, wiping a brow in the oppressive heat.

"He committed some serious mistakes, but he was protesting for the people, so it was right to give him a Christian burial rather than toss him to the dogs," added Marca, who has worked for 15 years at the cemetery.

Figuratively speaking, the government and mainly pro-goverment media are, however, stamping on Cerpa's grave. Villified as a deluded "terrorist criminal," they say his motives were purely egotistical -- ransom money and the freedom from jail of his wife Nancy Gilvonio.

The MRTA's insistence throughout the siege on the freedom of jailed comrades, including Gilvonio, contrasted with their nebulous statements in favour of an "economic reordering" and wealth redistribution.
The government has moved swiftly and effectively to prevent Cerpa from becoming a martyr and his tomb a shrine.

His body briefly disappeared, then re-appeared at the New Hope cemetery, meaning premature comparisons with Argentine-born revolutionary legend Che Guevara -- whose body is still unfound -- quickly died.

His small movement is virtually wiped-out, his tangible legacy questionable, and his all-or-nothing operation left him and his comrades dead. But after successfully capturing 500 of Peru's elite and holding the world on edge for four and a half months, it is doubtful the memory of Nestor Cerpa Cartolini will die soon.
"Cerpa is an actor who took the Oscar in world terrorism," said Peruvian guerrilla expert Carlos Tapia, adding that Mexico's Zapatista leader sub-commander Marcos "is a small-part actor at his side."
